title: Antivirals
summary: Drugs for herpesviruses, influenza, HIV, hepatitis B and C.

lessons.title: Antiherpes Drugs

levels.kid: Some germs called viruses hide inside your cells, like a burglar hiding in a house. Herpes viruses cause cold sores and chickenpox. The medicine acyclovir is a clever trick. It looks like a normal building block the virus uses to copy itself. But the virus has its own special tool that switches the medicine on. Healthy cells barely switch it on at all. Once it is on, the fake block gets stuck in the virus's copy and the copying stops, like a broken brick in a wall. That way the medicine mostly hurts the virus, not you. Doctors also have stronger medicines for tougher herpes viruses, but those can be harder on the body, so they are used carefully.
levels.hs:
Herpesviruses (HSV-1, HSV-2, varicella-zoster virus and cytomegalovirus, CMV) are DNA viruses that stay latent in the body for life. Antiviral drugs cannot remove latent virus; they stop active copying during an outbreak.

The main drug is **acyclovir**, which looks like guanosine, one of the building blocks of DNA. Its trick is selectivity: the virus's own enzyme, **thymidine kinase**, adds the first phosphate, and human enzymes then finish the job, making acyclovir triphosphate. That active form blocks the viral DNA polymerase and gets built into the growing DNA chain. Because it lacks the chemical hook (a 3'-OH group) needed to add the next building block, the chain stops. This is called **chain termination**.

**Valacyclovir** is a prodrug: the body turns it into acyclovir, and it is absorbed much better from the gut. **Famciclovir** works similarly via penciclovir.

CMV needs different drugs: **ganciclovir** (and its oral prodrug valganciclovir), which can suppress the bone marrow. If a virus becomes resistant, **foscarnet** and **cidofovir** are backups, but both can damage the kidneys.

For doctors, one of the most important uses is suspected herpes encephalitis, a brain infection treated with IV acyclovir right away.
levels.college:
**Nucleoside analog activation.** Acyclovir is an acyclic guanosine analog. HSV and VZV thymidine kinase (TK) performs the first, rate-limiting phosphorylation far more efficiently than host kinases; cellular guanylate kinase and other kinases then form acyclovir triphosphate. This triphosphate competitively inhibits viral DNA polymerase (it is preferred over host polymerases), is incorporated, and acts as an **obligate chain terminator** because the acyclic side chain has no 3'-OH. Infected cells trap the drug, so selectivity is high and toxicity low.

**Prodrugs.** Valacyclovir (L-valyl ester) is absorbed by intestinal peptide transporters and hydrolyzed to acyclovir, roughly tripling to quadrupling bioavailability. Famciclovir is converted to penciclovir, whose triphosphate has a longer intracellular half-life but is not an obligate chain terminator.

**CMV.** CMV lacks TK; ganciclovir is first phosphorylated by the CMV **UL97** protein kinase. Toxicity is myelosuppression (neutropenia) and it is a potential carcinogen and teratogen. Valganciclovir is its oral prodrug.

**Kinase-independent drugs.** Cidofovir is a nucleotide (phosphonate) analog: it already carries a phosphate mimic, so it skips the viral kinase and needs only host kinases. It is nephrotoxic (proximal tubule uptake via OAT1), so it is given with probenecid and saline. Foscarnet is a pyrophosphate analog that binds the polymerase's pyrophosphate site directly with no activation. It causes nephrotoxicity and electrolyte disturbances (low calcium, magnesium, potassium; abnormal phosphate) that can provoke seizures.

**Resistance.** Most acyclovir-resistant HSV in immunocompromised patients is TK-deficient or TK-altered; foscarnet is used. UL97 mutations cause ganciclovir resistance; UL54 polymerase mutations can cross-resist.

**Newer CMV agents.** Letermovir inhibits the terminase complex (UL56) and is used for prophylaxis after stem cell transplant; maribavir inhibits UL97 for refractory CMV.
levels.phd:
**Structural basis of selectivity.** HSV TK has unusually broad substrate tolerance (it phosphorylates thymidine, deoxycytidine and many acyclic nucleosides) while human cytosolic TK1 is highly specific. This promiscuity is the entire therapeutic window for acyclovir: uninfected cells form negligible triphosphate. After incorporation, acyclovir monophosphate at the primer terminus also traps the polymerase in a dead-end complex when the next templated dNTP binds, so inhibition is effectively irreversible for that enzyme molecule, a stronger effect than simple competitive inhibition.

**Penciclovir vs acyclovir.** Penciclovir triphosphate has lower affinity for the polymerase but a much longer intracellular half-life; its 3'-hydroxyl-equivalent permits limited further extension, making it a non-obligate terminator. Pharmacodynamically, the duration of intracellular triphosphate matters more than plasma half-life, a recurring theme in nucleoside pharmacology.

**CMV kinases and resistance genetics.** UL97 mutations cluster at codons 460, 520 and 590–607, reducing ganciclovir phosphorylation; UL54 mutations in conserved polymerase regions confer variable cross-resistance to ganciclovir, cidofovir and foscarnet. Maribavir competes with ATP at UL97, which means it **antagonizes** ganciclovir activation; the two are not co-administered. Letermovir targets the pUL56 terminase subunit that cleaves concatemeric DNA into unit-length genomes during packaging, a step with no human counterpart, explaining its favorable toxicity; resistance maps to UL56 (and UL89/UL51). It has no activity against HSV.

**Latency.** Neurotropic HSV and VZV maintain latent episomes in sensory ganglia with minimal lytic gene expression (the latency-associated transcript). No polymerase inhibitor touches this reservoir, which is why therapy shortens and suppresses but does not cure. Helicase-primase inhibitors (for example amenamevir, approved in Japan for zoster, and pritelivir in trials for resistant HSV) act independently of TK, offering a route around the dominant resistance mechanism.

**Toxicity mechanisms.** Acyclovir is poorly soluble; rapid IV infusion with low urine flow causes intratubular crystal nephropathy, and accumulation in renal failure produces neurotoxicity (tremor, confusion), often misread as encephalitis worsening.
levels.expert:
**Encephalitis first.** In any patient with fever, altered mental status, seizures or focal signs (especially temporal lobe changes on MRI or periodic lateralized discharges on EEG), start IV acyclovir empirically before the lumbar puncture result returns. HSV encephalitis mortality falls dramatically with early treatment, and a negative early HSV PCR on CSF does not exclude it if sampled within the first days; repeat the PCR when suspicion remains. Neurosurgeons meet this when a patient with a presumed temporal mass turns out to have necrotizing HSV encephalitis, so think about it before biopsy.

**Kidney safeguards.** Hydrate, infuse slowly, use ideal body weight in obesity and adjust for renal function. Watch creatinine on day two or three. In older patients with chronic kidney disease, new confusion on acyclovir or valacyclovir is drug neurotoxicity until proven otherwise; it improves with stopping the drug and, in severe cases, dialysis.

**Zoster.** Antivirals help most when started early, within roughly three days of rash. Herpes zoster ophthalmicus needs urgent ophthalmology review. Prevention with the recombinant zoster vaccine beats treatment.

**Transplant and HIV.** CMV strategy is either prophylaxis (letermovir after stem cell transplant; valganciclovir in many solid organ settings) or pre-emptive therapy guided by viral load PCR. Ganciclovir neutropenia is the common limiting toxicity, so check blood counts. Suspect resistance when viral load rises despite adequate therapy for about two weeks; send genotyping for UL97 and UL54 rather than guessing.

**Foscarnet in practice.** Pre-hydrate, monitor creatinine, calcium (ionized), magnesium, potassium and phosphate often, and warn nurses about paresthesias and seizures from acute ionized hypocalcemia. Genital ulcers can occur from drug concentrated in urine. Cidofovir requires probenecid and saline, and causes neutropenia and ocular hypotony.

Teach patients that recurrence is expected and that suppressive therapy reduces outbreaks and transmission but does not eliminate either.

keyPoints: Acyclovir is a guanosine analog first phosphorylated by viral thymidine kinase, then by host kinases
Acyclovir triphosphate inhibits viral DNA polymerase and is an obligate chain terminator (no 3'-OH)
Valacyclovir and valganciclovir are prodrugs with better oral bioavailability
Ganciclovir (CMV) is activated by UL97; main toxicity is myelosuppression
Foscarnet (pyrophosphate analog) and cidofovir (nucleotide analog) bypass viral kinases; both are nephrotoxic
Suspected HSV encephalitis: start IV acyclovir immediately

test.q: Which enzyme performs the first phosphorylation of acyclovir?
test.explain: HSV/VZV thymidine kinase adds the first phosphate; host kinases then make the triphosphate. Host guanylate kinase acts at the second step.

test.q: Why is acyclovir a chain terminator?
choices: It lacks a 3'-OH group to attach the next nucleotide
test.explain: With no 3'-hydroxyl, no further nucleotide can be added after incorporation.

test.q: Valacyclovir differs from acyclovir mainly because it:
choices: Has much higher oral bioavailability as a prodrug
test.explain: The valine ester is absorbed by intestinal peptide transporters and converted to acyclovir.

test.q: Ganciclovir is phosphorylated in CMV-infected cells by:
test.explain: CMV has no thymidine kinase; UL97 protein kinase does the first step.

test.q: The dose-limiting toxicity of ganciclovir is:
test.explain: Bone marrow suppression, especially neutropenia, is the classic limiting toxicity.

test.q: Which drug is a pyrophosphate analog that requires no activation?
test.explain: Foscarnet binds the polymerase pyrophosphate site directly.

test.q: Foscarnet can cause seizures mainly through:
test.explain: Foscarnet chelates divalent cations and causes electrolyte loss.

test.q: Cidofovir is given with probenecid to:
test.explain: Probenecid blocks OAT1-mediated tubular uptake of cidofovir.

test.q: Name the IV drug started immediately for suspected herpes simplex encephalitis.
test.explain: Early empiric IV acyclovir saves lives and brain tissue.

test.q: Herpes viruses persist in sensory ganglia in a state called ___, which antivirals cannot eliminate.
test.explain: Latent episomes have minimal replication, so polymerase inhibitors cannot touch them.

test.q: Most acyclovir-resistant HSV has a defect in which viral enzyme?
test.explain: TK-deficient or altered mutants cannot activate acyclovir.

test.q: Letermovir prevents CMV disease by inhibiting the viral ___ complex.
test.explain: It blocks cleavage and packaging of viral DNA.

kidTest.q: What kind of germ is herpes?
kidTest.explain: Herpes is a virus that hides in our cells.

kidTest.q: Acyclovir is switched on mostly by:
kidTest.explain: The virus's special enzyme turns the medicine on.

kidTest.q: What happens when the fake block gets into the virus copy?
kidTest.explain: Like a broken brick, it stops the wall from being built.

kidTest.q: Why does acyclovir mostly hurt the virus and not you?
choices: Healthy cells barely switch it on
kidTest.explain: Only infected cells activate much of the drug.

kidTest.q: What medicine is used for cold sores and chickenpox? (starts with 'a')
kidTest.explain: Acyclovir is the classic herpes medicine.

advancedTest.q: Why are maribavir and ganciclovir not combined?
choices: Maribavir inhibits UL97 and so blocks ganciclovir activation
advancedTest.explain: Ganciclovir needs UL97 for its first phosphorylation; maribavir inhibits that kinase.

advancedTest.q: Penciclovir differs from acyclovir in that its triphosphate:
choices: Is an obligate terminator with short half-life
Has a longer intracellular half-life and is a non-obligate terminator
advancedTest.explain: Its hydroxyl equivalent allows limited extension; prolonged intracellular persistence compensates for lower affinity.

advancedTest.q: A transplant patient's CMV viral load rises after two weeks of adequate ganciclovir. Best next step?
advancedTest.explain: Genotyping guides choice among foscarnet, cidofovir or maribavir.

advancedTest.q: Why does letermovir have no activity against HSV yet low host toxicity?
choices: Its target, the pUL56 terminase, is CMV-specific and has no human counterpart
advancedTest.explain: Terminase is unique to herpesvirus genome packaging and differs among herpesviruses.

lessons.title: Influenza and Respiratory Antivirals

levels.kid: The flu virus is like a tiny robber. It sneaks into a cell, makes lots of copies, and then the copies try to leave and rob more cells. To leave, they cut themselves free with a pair of scissors. The flu medicine oseltamivir takes away those scissors, so the new viruses stay stuck to the cell and cannot spread. Another flu medicine breaks the copying machine instead. These medicines work best when you start them early, soon after you feel sick. Doctors also have medicines for other breathing viruses, like the one that causes COVID-19, and special shots that protect babies from RSV. The best plan of all is still the flu vaccine, which teaches your body to fight first.
levels.hs:
Respiratory viruses like influenza, RSV and SARS-CoV-2 are RNA viruses, and each family has its own drug targets.

**Influenza.** New flu viruses bud from the cell surface but stay stuck to sialic acid on the cell until the viral enzyme **neuraminidase** cuts them free. **Neuraminidase inhibitors** (oseltamivir, a pill; zanamivir, inhaled; peramivir, IV) block that release, so the infection spreads more slowly. **Baloxavir** works earlier, blocking the viral enzyme that steals caps from human messenger RNA ('cap-snatching') so the virus cannot make its own proteins. Older drugs, **amantadine** and **rimantadine**, blocked the M2 channel, but nearly all current flu A strains are resistant, so they are no longer used for flu.

Flu drugs shorten illness by about a day in healthy people when started early, ideally within 48 hours. In hospitalized or high-risk patients, doctors treat no matter how long symptoms have lasted.

**COVID-19.** Nirmatrelvir blocks the virus's main protease and is packaged with ritonavir, which slows its breakdown in the liver (and causes many drug interactions). Remdesivir is an IV drug that jams the viral RNA polymerase.

**RSV.** Long-acting antibodies like nirsevimab protect infants through RSV season.
levels.college:
**Neuraminidase inhibitors (NAIs).** Oseltamivir phosphate is an ethyl ester prodrug hydrolyzed by hepatic carboxylesterase 1 to oseltamivir carboxylate, a transition-state analog of sialic acid that binds the conserved NA active site of influenza A and B. Zanamivir has poor oral bioavailability and is inhaled (avoid in asthma/COPD: bronchospasm). Peramivir is given IV. NAIs prevent release and promote aggregation of progeny virions. Adverse effects: nausea and vomiting (oseltamivir); neuropsychiatric events have been reported, mainly in children, though causality is uncertain. Renal elimination requires adjustment.

**Baloxavir marboxil** is a prodrug of baloxavir acid, which inhibits the cap-dependent endonuclease of the polymerase acidic (PA) subunit, blocking cap-snatching and viral mRNA synthesis. It reduces viral shedding faster than oseltamivir. The PA I38T substitution reduces susceptibility and emerges more often in children. Absorption is reduced by polyvalent cations (chelation).

**Adamantanes** block the M2 proton channel needed for viral uncoating in the endosome. The S31N mutation is nearly universal in circulating influenza A; influenza B lacks M2. Amantadine persists as an antiparkinsonian agent.

**SARS-CoV-2.** Nirmatrelvir is a covalent peptidomimetic inhibitor of the main protease (Mpro/3CLpro) that cleaves the viral polyproteins; ritonavir is a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor used only as a **pharmacokinetic booster**. Remdesivir is a monophosphoramidate (ProTide) adenosine analog; its triphosphate is incorporated by RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) and causes delayed chain termination. Molnupiravir's active form is incorporated into viral RNA and induces error catastrophe (lethal mutagenesis).

**RSV.** Nirsevimab is an extended half-life monoclonal antibody to the prefusion F protein; palivizumab is older. Aerosolized ribavirin is rarely used and is teratogenic.
levels.phd:
**NAI structure-activity and resistance.** Zanamivir retains a glycerol side chain and a guanidino group that mimic sialic acid closely, whereas oseltamivir replaces the glycerol with a pentyl ether that requires a conformational rearrangement of Glu276 to open a hydrophobic pocket. This explains why the **H275Y** (N1 numbering) substitution, which hinders that rearrangement, confers high-level oseltamivir resistance while largely sparing zanamivir. Seasonal H1N1 acquired H275Y globally in 2007–2008 because permissive secondary mutations restored fitness, a lesson that resistance can spread without drug pressure once compensatory epistasis is in place.

**Cap-snatching.** The influenza polymerase is a heterotrimer (PB1, PB2, PA). PB2 binds the 5' cap of host pre-mRNA; the PA endonuclease, a two-metal (Mn²⁺) active site enzyme, cleaves 10–13 nucleotides downstream; PB1 extends the primer. Baloxavir acid chelates the two metal ions, which is also why di- and trivalent cations in food or antacids reduce absorption. Because it targets a step upstream of protein synthesis, it reduces viral titers more steeply than NAIs.

**Nucleoside analogs for RNA viruses.** Coronaviruses encode an exonuclease (nsp14 ExoN) that proofreads, excising many classic chain terminators. Remdesivir escapes partly because, after incorporation, synthesis continues for three more nucleotides before steric clash with the polymerase stalls it (delayed termination) and the analog becomes buried beyond easy excision. Molnupiravir's metabolite exists in tautomers that pair with either G or A, seeding mutations in later rounds, an approach with theoretical mutagenic concerns for host cells that limited enthusiasm.

**Host targeting.** Host-directed antivirals (for example, inhibitors of endosomal acidification or of host proteases like TMPRSS2) promise higher genetic barriers but tend to fail on toxicity and redundancy, a recurring trade-off.

**Antibody escape.** Monoclonals against SARS-CoV-2 spike lost activity as variants emerged; RSV F epitopes are more conserved, but nirsevimab-resistant site Ø variants are under surveillance.
levels.expert:
**Who to treat for influenza.** Treat anyone hospitalized, severely ill, or at high risk (young children, older adults, pregnancy, immunosuppression, chronic heart, lung, kidney or neurologic disease) as soon as possible, regardless of symptom duration, and do not wait for test results when flu is circulating. Healthy outpatients benefit modestly, mostly if started within two days. Oseltamivir is the default in hospital; baloxavir is an outpatient option, and IV peramivir or zanamivir covers patients who cannot take oral drugs.

**Pitfalls.** Vomiting on oseltamivir is common and limits adherence; give it with food. Inhaled zanamivir is not used in mechanically ventilated patients because the lactose carrier can clog the circuit. Antacids and calcium blunt baloxavir. Patients who received live attenuated influenza vaccine around the time of antiviral use may have reduced vaccine effect. Post-exposure prophylaxis matters in nursing homes during outbreaks.

**Neurologic angle.** Influenza can cause encephalopathy in children, and severe cases deserve early antiviral therapy and ICU care. Amantadine is used in neurocritical care to speed recovery of consciousness after traumatic brain injury, supported by a randomized trial, a separate indication from influenza.

**COVID-19 in practice.** Nirmatrelvir-ritonavir is effective in high-risk outpatients, but ritonavir's CYP3A inhibition is the main clinical problem: run every medication list through an interaction checker. Tacrolimus levels can rise to toxic ranges, some antiarrhythmics and statins must be held, and certain drugs make it contraindicated. Remdesivir is used in hospitalized patients needing oxygen and in high-risk outpatients when oral options are unsuitable.

**RSV.** Infants receive nirsevimab or are protected through maternal vaccination; older adults now have RSV vaccines. Treatment of established RSV is mainly supportive.

And always: vaccination beats any antiviral.

keyPoints: Neuraminidase inhibitors (oseltamivir, zanamivir, peramivir) block release of new influenza virions
Baloxavir inhibits the PA cap-dependent endonuclease (cap-snatching)
Adamantanes (M2 blockers) are obsolete for influenza due to near-universal resistance
Treat hospitalized or high-risk flu patients regardless of symptom duration; others benefit most within 48 hours
Nirmatrelvir (Mpro inhibitor) is boosted by ritonavir, a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor with many interactions
Remdesivir is an adenosine analog prodrug causing delayed chain termination of RdRp

examples.src: A patient on tacrolimus gets nirmatrelvir-ritonavir
examples.tr: Ritonavir blocks CYP3A4, so tacrolimus can accumulate to toxic levels unless managed.
Zanamivir usually remains active because it binds without the Glu276 rearrangement.

lessons.title: HIV: Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitors

levels.kid: HIV is a virus that hides inside the body's guard cells, the ones that fight germs. HIV writes its instructions in a different language than our cells, so it uses a special machine to translate them. That machine is called reverse transcriptase. Some medicines give the machine fake letters, so the copy breaks halfway. Other medicines jam a stick into the side of the machine so it cannot move. Doctors always use a team of medicines together, because the virus is sneaky and can learn to beat one medicine alone, but it cannot beat a whole team. With these medicines, people with HIV can live long, healthy lives.
levels.hs:
HIV is a retrovirus: its genes are stored as RNA, but it must turn them into DNA to join the host cell's chromosomes. The enzyme that does this is **reverse transcriptase (RT)**, and it makes lots of mistakes, which is why HIV mutates so fast.

Two drug classes block RT:
- **NRTIs** (nucleoside/nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitors), like tenofovir, emtricitabine, lamivudine and abacavir. They are fake DNA building blocks. Human enzymes add phosphates to activate them, RT builds them into the DNA, and because they lack a 3'-OH group, the DNA chain stops.
- **NNRTIs** (non-nucleoside RT inhibitors), like efavirenz, rilpivirine and doravirine. They bind a pocket next to RT's active site and bend the enzyme out of shape.

HIV treatment uses **combination antiretroviral therapy**, usually three drugs from at least two classes (or two very strong drugs). That makes resistance very unlikely. Treatment keeps the virus undetectable, lets the immune system recover, and means the person cannot pass HIV to sexual partners (often summarized as Undetectable = Untransmittable).

Side effects differ by drug: tenofovir can affect kidneys and bones, abacavir can cause a dangerous allergic reaction in people with a certain gene, and efavirenz can cause vivid dreams and dizziness.
levels.college:
**NRTIs.** All are prodrugs requiring stepwise phosphorylation by **host** kinases (no viral kinase is involved) to triphosphates that compete with natural dNTPs and terminate the chain. Tenofovir is a nucleotide (acyclic phosphonate) analog, so it needs only two phosphorylations. Two prodrugs exist: tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) gives high plasma tenofovir (renal proximal tubulopathy, bone mineral density loss), while tenofovir alafenamide (TAF) is more stable in plasma and is cleaved intracellularly (cathepsin A in lymphocytes), giving much lower plasma levels and less kidney and bone toxicity but slightly more weight gain and lipid change.

Cytidine analogs **lamivudine (3TC)** and **emtricitabine (FTC)** are very well tolerated. The **M184V** mutation confers high-level resistance to both but reduces viral fitness and increases susceptibility to tenofovir and zidovudine.

**Abacavir** (guanosine analog) causes a hypersensitivity reaction (fever, rash, GI and respiratory symptoms) strongly associated with **HLA-B*57:01**; screen before starting and never rechallenge. **Zidovudine (AZT)** causes bone marrow suppression (anemia with macrocytosis) and myopathy.

**Mitochondrial toxicity.** NRTIs variably inhibit mitochondrial DNA polymerase γ, causing lactic acidosis, hepatic steatosis, neuropathy, lipoatrophy and pancreatitis. This was severe with older 'd-drugs' (stavudine, didanosine) that are no longer used.

**NNRTIs** bind a hydrophobic allosteric pocket about 10 Å from the polymerase active site; they are non-competitive, need no activation, and do not act on HIV-2. A single mutation (K103N) causes efavirenz and nevirapine resistance (low genetic barrier). Efavirenz: CNS effects and CYP induction; nevirapine: hepatotoxicity and severe rash; rilpivirine requires stomach acid (PPIs contraindicated); doravirine has fewer interactions and lipid effects.

**HBV overlap.** Tenofovir, emtricitabine and lamivudine also suppress HBV; stopping them in coinfected patients can trigger a hepatitis flare.
levels.phd:
**Structural pharmacology of RT.** HIV-1 RT is a p66/p51 heterodimer; only p66 carries polymerase and RNase H active sites. The NNRTI-binding pocket does not exist in the apo enzyme; it forms when the drug binds, displacing Tyr181 and Tyr188 and repositioning the 'primer grip' (β12–β14) and the catalytic aspartates (YMDD motif), slowing chemistry rather than blocking dNTP binding. Second-generation diarylpyrimidines (etravirine, rilpivirine) are torsionally flexible ('wiggling and jiggling'), letting them re-adapt to pockets mutated at K103N or Y181C, which raised the genetic barrier.

**Two resistance mechanisms for NRTIs.** Discrimination mutations (M184V, K65R) let RT exclude the analog during incorporation; M184V's β-branched valine clashes sterically with the oxathiolane ring of 3TC/FTC. Excision mutations, the **thymidine analog mutations (TAMs)** such as M41L, D67N, K70R, T215Y/F, enhance ATP-mediated pyrophosphorolysis that removes an incorporated terminator, restoring the primer. M184V and K65R reduce excision, explaining the clinically exploited **hypersusceptibility** and antagonism between resistance pathways.

**Intracellular pharmacology.** Efficacy tracks intracellular triphosphate and its ratio to competing dNTPs rather than plasma levels. Resting CD4 cells have low dNTP pools (partly through SAMHD1), which favors analogs, while activated cells differ; tenofovir diphosphate has a very long intracellular half-life in PBMCs and red cells, which is why dried blood spot levels serve as adherence markers in PrEP studies.

**HLA-B*57:01 and abacavir.** Abacavir binds the peptide-binding groove of HLA-B*57:01 and alters the repertoire of self-peptides presented, generating neo-self epitopes that activate T cells: the 'altered peptide repertoire' model. It is a landmark example of a pharmacogenomic test that essentially eliminated an immunologic adverse reaction (PREDICT-1 trial).

**Translocation inhibition.** Nucleoside RT translocation inhibitors such as islatravir keep a 3'-OH but block translocation through a 4'-ethynyl group; development was slowed by dose-related lymphocyte decreases, showing how unexpected off-target effects can derail a mechanistically elegant class.
levels.expert:
**Starting therapy.** Current guidelines start antiretroviral therapy for everyone with HIV, as soon as possible after diagnosis (often the same day) unless specific opportunistic infections warrant a delay. Common initial regimens pair an integrase inhibitor with two NRTIs (for example, a tenofovir prodrug plus emtricitabine or lamivudine) or use a two-drug regimen in selected patients without HBV and with low viral load.

**Before prescribing an NRTI backbone.** Check HBV status: if positive, the regimen must include tenofovir plus emtricitabine or lamivudine, and stopping them can cause a fatal HBV flare. Screen HLA-B*57:01 before abacavir. Check creatinine, urinalysis (glucose and protein for proximal tubulopathy) and bone risk before TDF; choose TAF in kidney disease or osteoporosis. Send baseline resistance genotyping, since transmitted NNRTI resistance (K103N) is the most common.

**NNRTI pearls.** Efavirenz's neuropsychiatric effects (vivid dreams, dizziness, depression, and in some patients late-onset neurotoxicity) made it fall out of favor; it is a CYP3A and CYP2B6 inducer, and CYP2B6 slow metabolizers have higher levels. Rilpivirine needs a meal and fails with PPIs. Rilpivirine is also partnered with cabotegravir in long-acting injectable therapy for suppressed patients.

**Neurologic and neurosurgical relevance.** Peripheral neuropathy in people with HIV can be HIV-related or from old d-drugs. HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder and CNS escape (virus in CSF despite plasma suppression) are reasons to consider CNS penetration and resistance testing of CSF. For a ring-enhancing brain lesion in advanced HIV, think toxoplasmosis versus primary CNS lymphoma before biopsy.

**Adherence is the drug.** Viral rebound almost always reflects missed doses, interactions or absorption problems before resistance. Ask nonjudgmentally, check interactions (rifampin, anticonvulsants, polyvalent cations for integrase partners) and simplify regimens.

NRTIs are activated by host kinases and cause chain termination; tenofovir is a nucleotide analog
TDF has more renal/bone toxicity than TAF; abacavir requires HLA-B*57:01 screening
M184V causes 3TC/FTC resistance but reduces fitness and increases tenofovir susceptibility
NNRTIs bind an allosteric pocket, need no activation, have a low genetic barrier (K103N) and do not work on HIV-2
Tenofovir, emtricitabine and lamivudine also treat HBV; stopping them can cause a hepatitis flare

lessons.title: HIV: Protease, Integrase and Entry Inhibitors

levels.kid: HIV has a step-by-step plan, like building a toy. First it has to open the door of a cell and get in. Then it glues its own instructions into the cell's instruction book. Last, it builds new viruses and cuts the pieces apart with scissors so they work. Doctors have medicines that stop each step. Entry blockers lock the door. Integrase blockers take away the glue, so the instructions cannot stick. Protease blockers take away the scissors, so the new viruses are broken and cannot hurt more cells. Using medicines that stop different steps at the same time is like putting three locks on a door.
levels.hs:
HIV's life cycle has many steps, and each is a drug target:

1. **Attachment and entry.** The viral protein gp120 grabs the CD4 receptor on a T cell and then a co-receptor (CCR5 or CXCR4). Then gp41 fuses the virus with the cell. **Maraviroc** blocks CCR5, **enfuvirtide** blocks gp41 fusion, and **fostemsavir** and **ibalizumab** block attachment.
2. **Reverse transcription** (last lesson).
3. **Integration.** The enzyme **integrase** cuts the viral DNA and pastes it into the cell's chromosome. **Integrase inhibitors** like dolutegravir and bictegravir block this. They are now the backbone of most first regimens because they are powerful and well tolerated.
4. **Assembly and maturation.** The virus makes long protein chains that **protease** must cut into working parts. **Protease inhibitors** like darunavir leave new viruses immature and non-infectious. They are usually 'boosted' with ritonavir or cobicistat, drugs that slow liver breakdown so levels stay high.

New long-acting options include the capsid inhibitor **lenacapavir** and injectable cabotegravir. Some of these drugs are also used for **PrEP**, which prevents HIV in people who don't have it.

Side effects: integrase inhibitors can cause weight gain; boosters cause many drug interactions.
levels.college:
**Protease inhibitors (PIs).** HIV protease is a C2-symmetric aspartyl protease homodimer that cleaves Gag and Gag-Pol polyproteins. PIs are peptidomimetic transition-state analogs (hydroxyethylene or hydroxyethylamine cores). They have poor oral bioavailability and extensive CYP3A4 metabolism, so they are co-administered with a **pharmacokinetic booster**: low-level ritonavir or cobicistat (cobicistat has no antiviral activity). Darunavir has a high genetic barrier; atazanavir inhibits UGT1A1, causing benign indirect hyperbilirubinemia, and needs gastric acid. Older PIs caused dyslipidemia, insulin resistance and lipodystrophy.

**Integrase strand transfer inhibitors (INSTIs).** Integrase performs 3' processing and strand transfer; INSTIs (raltegravir, elvitegravir, dolutegravir, bictegravir, cabotegravir) bind the intasome active site by chelating the two Mg²⁺ ions and displace the viral DNA 3' end. Consequences of chelation: polyvalent cations (aluminum/magnesium antacids, calcium, iron, zinc) reduce absorption, so doses must be separated or taken with food. Dolutegravir and bictegravir inhibit renal OCT2/MATE1, raising serum creatinine without changing true GFR. Weight gain is a class concern. Dolutegravir and bictegravir have high resistance barriers.

**Entry inhibitors.** Maraviroc is an allosteric CCR5 antagonist effective only against CCR5-tropic virus; a **tropism assay** is required first. Enfuvirtide is a 36-amino-acid peptide that binds gp41 HR1, preventing six-helix bundle formation; it is injected and causes injection-site reactions. Ibalizumab is a CD4 domain 2 monoclonal antibody that blocks post-attachment conformational changes without immunosuppression. Fostemsavir is a prodrug of temsavir, which binds gp120 and locks it in a closed state.

**Capsid inhibitors.** Lenacapavir binds between capsid subunits, disrupting nuclear import, assembly and capsid formation; its extremely slow release from subcutaneous depots supports long-acting use in treatment-experienced patients and PrEP.

**Booster interactions** are the main pitfall: inhaled or injected corticosteroids metabolized by CYP3A (fluticasone, triamcinolone) can cause iatrogenic Cushing syndrome.
levels.phd:
**Intasome pharmacology.** Retroviral integrase functions as a multimeric intasome assembled on viral DNA ends. INSTIs bind only the DNA-bound complex, with their halogenated benzyl group stacking against the penultimate cytosine of the processed 3' end and their metal-binding triad coordinating both catalytic Mg²⁺ ions. Second-generation INSTIs have longer linkers and dissociate far more slowly (dissociative half-lives of many hours), which correlates with their higher genetic barrier. Raltegravir resistance pathways (Y143, Q148, N155) and cross-resistance to dolutegravir require Q148 plus additional mutations; the near absence of emergent resistance with dolutegravir in treatment-naive patients is a striking feature still debated mechanistically (fitness cost, residence time).

**Protease substrate envelope.** Drug-resistant protease mutations accumulate where inhibitors protrude beyond the volume occupied by natural substrates. Darunavir was designed to stay within this 'substrate envelope' and to make backbone hydrogen bonds (via its bis-tetrahydrofuran group) to conserved main-chain atoms, which side-chain mutations cannot easily abolish, explaining its robust barrier. It also inhibits protease dimerization.

**Booster pharmacology.** Ritonavir is a mechanism-based CYP3A4 inactivator but also induces CYP1A2, 2B6, 2C9, 2C19 and glucuronidation via PXR, so net effects are drug-specific and time-dependent. Cobicistat is a more selective CYP3A inhibitor without the induction profile, though it inhibits renal MATE1 and transporters.

**Co-receptor biology.** CCR5Δ32 homozygosity protects against R5-tropic HIV, the basis of maraviroc and of the 'Berlin' and 'London' patients cured after stem-cell transplants from CCR5Δ32 donors. Tropism switching to CXCR4 tends to occur late and predicts faster progression; maraviroc failure often reflects outgrowth of pre-existing X4 minorities.

**Capsid as target.** Lenacapavir binds the FG-binding pocket used by host factors CPSF6 and Nup153, hyperstabilizing the lattice and blocking nuclear entry. Its picomolar potency and solubility profile enable depot release over months, reframing adherence as a pharmacokinetic engineering problem. Reservoir persistence in latently infected resting memory CD4 cells remains the barrier to cure.
levels.expert:
**Regimen logic.** For most treatment-naive adults, an INSTI (bictegravir or dolutegravir) plus a two-NRTI backbone is first choice: high potency, high barrier, few interactions. Darunavir with a booster is reserved for situations where resistance is uncertain (rapid start before genotype, poor adherence history) because of its barrier, but it brings interaction burden. Dolutegravir with lamivudine is an option without HBV, without known resistance and with lower viral loads.

**Interactions you will actually see.** Boosted regimens raise levels of many statins, anticoagulants, antiarrhythmics, some antiepileptics, inhaled steroids and sedatives like midazolam. Neurosurgical anesthesia and ICU sedation in a patient on a boosted regimen need a pharmacist review. Conversely, enzyme-inducing antiseizure drugs (carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital) and rifampin can drop INSTI and PI levels and cause virologic failure; levetiracetam is a cleaner choice for seizure prophylaxis. Separate INSTIs from antacids, calcium and iron, or take them together with food per labeling.

**Creatinine trap.** A small creatinine rise after starting dolutegravir, bictegravir or cobicistat reflects tubular secretion inhibition, not kidney injury; it plateaus early. Progressive rises suggest true injury, often from TDF.

**Weight and metabolism.** INSTIs and TAF are linked to weight gain, especially in women and Black patients; counsel early. Pregnancy: dolutegravir is now preferred after early neural tube signals were not confirmed.

**Prevention.** Oral PrEP (TDF/FTC or TAF/FTC in some groups) and long-acting injectables (cabotegravir, lenacapavir) are highly effective. Test for HIV before and during PrEP: starting it in someone with unrecognized acute HIV selects resistance. Post-exposure prophylaxis must start as soon as possible, ideally within hours and not later than 72 hours.

**Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome** can unmask cryptococcal or TB meningitis after starting therapy; in cryptococcal meningitis, ART is deliberately delayed a few weeks.

keyPoints: Life cycle targets: entry (maraviroc, enfuvirtide, fostemsavir, ibalizumab), integration (INSTIs), maturation (PIs), capsid (lenacapavir)
INSTIs chelate Mg²⁺ in integrase; polyvalent cations reduce absorption
Dolutegravir/bictegravir raise creatinine via OCT2/MATE1 inhibition without lowering GFR
PIs are boosted by ritonavir or cobicistat (CYP3A inhibition), causing many interactions
Maraviroc requires a tropism assay showing CCR5-tropic virus
Atazanavir causes benign indirect hyperbilirubinemia via UGT1A1 inhibition

lessons.title: Hepatitis B and C Antivirals

levels.kid: Hepatitis means the liver is sore and swollen, and two viruses called hepatitis B and hepatitis C can cause it. Hepatitis C is like a weed with shallow roots: new medicines pull it out completely, and most people are cured in a few months. Hepatitis B is trickier. It hides a tiny copy of itself deep inside the liver cell's control room, like a weed with a root you cannot reach. Medicines can stop it from growing, but the hidden root usually stays, so people often keep taking them for a long time. A vaccine can stop hepatitis B before it ever starts, which is why babies get it.
levels.hs:
**Hepatitis C (HCV)** is an RNA virus that copies itself in the cytoplasm and never enters the nucleus, so if you stop it, it's gone. Modern **direct-acting antivirals (DAAs)** cure more than 95% of people with a short course of pills. Each targets a viral protein:
- **NS3/4A protease inhibitors** (names end in -previr, like glecaprevir)
- **NS5A inhibitors** (-asvir, like velpatasvir)
- **NS5B polymerase inhibitors** (-buvir, like sofosbuvir)
Doctors combine two or three classes. 'Cure' is called a sustained virologic response: no virus in the blood months after treatment ends.

**Hepatitis B (HBV)** is a DNA virus that makes a stable circle of DNA (cccDNA) in the liver cell nucleus. Drugs like **entecavir** and **tenofovir** block the HBV polymerase (which works as a reverse transcriptase) and keep the virus suppressed, protecting the liver from scarring and cancer. But they rarely remove cccDNA, so treatment is usually long-term. Interferon is a finite option that boosts immunity but has many side effects.

Important safety point: if someone has both HBV and HCV, curing HCV can make HBV flare, so doctors check for HBV first.
levels.college:
**HCV life cycle and DAAs.** HCV's positive-sense RNA is translated into a polyprotein cleaved by host and viral proteases. **NS3/4A** (serine protease with cofactor NS4A) also cleaves host MAVS and TRIF, blunting interferon signaling; protease inhibitors (glecaprevir, grazoprevir, voxilaprevir) restore this. **NS5A** has no enzymatic activity; it organizes the replication complex ('membranous web') and virion assembly; NS5A inhibitors (ledipasvir, velpatasvir, pibrentasvir, elbasvir) are picomolar potent. **NS5B** is the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase: **sofosbuvir** is a uridine nucleotide ProTide prodrug activated in hepatocytes to a triphosphate chain terminator with a high resistance barrier; dasabuvir was a non-nucleoside NS5B inhibitor.

Pan-genotypic regimens: sofosbuvir/velpatasvir and glecaprevir/pibrentasvir; sofosbuvir/velpatasvir/voxilaprevir for retreatment. Protease inhibitors are contraindicated in decompensated cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B/C) because of hepatic metabolism and hepatotoxicity. Sofosbuvir with amiodarone can cause severe bradycardia. Ribavirin (guanosine analog; hemolytic anemia, teratogenic) is now an add-on in select cases.

**HBV.** HBV replicates through an RNA intermediate (pregenomic RNA) reverse-transcribed by its polymerase inside capsids. Nucleos(t)ide analogs (NAs): **entecavir** (guanosine analog; high barrier but reduced efficacy after lamivudine resistance) and **tenofovir** (TDF or TAF) are first line; lamivudine, adefovir and telbivudine are obsolete because of resistance (YMDD mutations) or toxicity. NAs suppress HBV DNA but rarely clear HBsAg because cccDNA and integrated DNA persist. **Pegylated interferon alfa** gives higher HBsAg loss in some, finite duration, but causes flu-like illness, cytopenias, depression and thyroid disease.

**Hepatitis D** requires HBsAg; bulevirtide blocks the NTCP entry receptor (approved in Europe).

**Boxed warnings:** HBV reactivation during HCV DAA therapy in coinfection, and severe flares after stopping NAs.
levels.phd:
**Why HCV is curable and HBV is not.** HCV has no nuclear or integrated reservoir; its replication complexes in ER-derived double-membrane vesicles depend on continuous synthesis, so suppression below a threshold for weeks eradicates infection. HBV forms cccDNA, a minichromosome assembled with host histones, replenished by intracellular recycling of nucleocapsids and resistant to NAs, which act downstream at reverse transcription. Integrated HBV DNA fragments also express HBsAg independently of cccDNA, which explains persistent antigenemia in HBeAg-negative disease and complicates 'functional cure' (sustained HBsAg loss off treatment) as an endpoint.

**NS5A inhibitor mechanism.** Despite picomolar EC₅₀ values, NS5A inhibitors bind a dimeric domain I interface and appear to block formation of new replication complexes rather than existing ones, consistent with their rapid early viral decline modeled as a second-phase effect on assembly. Symmetric dimeric structures (daclatasvir's twin imidazole-proline motif) mirror their target's symmetry. Resistance-associated substitutions (Y93H, L31M) can persist for years because they carry little fitness cost, unlike NS3 variants, which fade.

**Sofosbuvir's barrier.** S282T in NS5B confers resistance but cripples replication fitness, so it is rarely seen clinically. The 2'-fluoro-2'-C-methyl uridine design was chosen to resist mammalian polymerase incorporation, and the ProTide approach bypasses the inefficient first phosphorylation; hepatic first-pass delivery concentrates the active triphosphate where the virus is.

**Novel HBV approaches.** Capsid assembly modulators misdirect capsid formation; siRNAs (and antisense oligonucleotides such as bepirovirsen) silence transcripts from both cccDNA and integrated DNA, lowering HBsAg to release T-cell exhaustion; TLR7/8 agonists and checkpoint blockade aim to restore immune control; CRISPR and base-editing approaches target cccDNA directly. Combination strategies are likely needed, analogous to the evolution of HCV therapy.

**Bulevirtide** is a myristoylated preS1 lipopeptide that competes with HBV/HDV binding to NTCP, a bile acid transporter, and raises plasma bile acids as an on-target effect.
levels.expert:
**HCV in practice.** Screen every adult at least once and pregnant patients each pregnancy. Before treatment: genotype is often unnecessary with pan-genotypic regimens; assess fibrosis (elastography or a serum index), check HBV (HBsAg, anti-HBc), HIV, pregnancy, and every interaction. Acid suppressants reduce ledipasvir and velpatasvir absorption; enzyme inducers (carbamazepine, phenytoin, rifampin, St John's wort) are contraindicated; amiodarone with sofosbuvir can cause fatal bradycardia. In decompensated cirrhosis avoid protease inhibitors and involve a hepatologist. Confirm cure with an RNA test after treatment. Cure does not erase cirrhosis: patients with advanced fibrosis still need liver cancer surveillance. Reinfection is possible; cure is not immunity.

**HBV in practice.** Decide to treat using HBV DNA, ALT, HBeAg status and fibrosis; cirrhosis with detectable DNA is treated regardless of ALT. Entecavir or tenofovir are first line; choose TAF or entecavir with kidney or bone disease, and avoid entecavir after lamivudine resistance. In pregnancy with high viral load, tenofovir in the third trimester plus infant vaccination and immunoglobulin prevents transmission.

**Reactivation is a neurosurgery and ICU issue too.** Before rituximab, chemotherapy, high-intensity corticosteroids or transplant, test HBsAg and anti-HBc. Positive patients get prophylactic entecavir or tenofovir, because reactivation can cause fulminant hepatitis. Prolonged dexamethasone after brain tumor surgery counts as meaningful immunosuppression in this risk assessment.

**Stopping NAs** can trigger severe flares; never stop them casually, and monitor closely if planned discontinuation is attempted.

**Hepatitis D**: test HBsAg-positive patients for HDV antibody; it accelerates cirrhosis.

Prevention wins: universal HBV vaccination has cut childhood infection dramatically, and screening, linkage to care and treatment as prevention are central to HCV elimination.

keyPoints: HCV DAAs target NS3/4A protease (-previr), NS5A (-asvir) and NS5B polymerase (-buvir); cure rates exceed 95%
Sofosbuvir is a uridine nucleotide prodrug and chain terminator; avoid with amiodarone (bradycardia)
Protease inhibitors are contraindicated in decompensated cirrhosis
HBV is suppressed by entecavir or tenofovir but rarely cured because cccDNA persists
HBV can reactivate during HCV treatment or immunosuppression; screen HBsAg and anti-HBc
Stopping HBV nucleos(t)ide analogs can cause severe hepatitis flares
